title: GOD ASKED BALAAM, “WHO ARE THESE MEN WITH YOU?” — BUT THE REAL DANGER WAS WHAT BALAAM WAS HIDING IN HIS HEART
paragraphs: GOD ASKED BALAAM, “WHO ARE THESE MEN WITH YOU?” — BUT THE REAL DANGER WAS WHAT BALAAM WAS HIDING IN HIS HEART

When God asks a question He already knows the answer to, sometimes He is exposing something we refuse to admit. The terrifying story of Balaam reveals how a person can hear God's voice, speak spiritual words, and still be dangerously attracted to what God has forbidden.
“And God came unto Balaam, and said, What men are these with thee?” — Numbers 22:9 (KJV)
Imagine being awakened in the middle of the night by the voice of Almighty God.
Not because you were praying.
Not because you were worshiping.
But because certain people had entered your life, carrying an invitation that could change everything.
An invitation wrapped in opportunity.
An invitation accompanied by promises of honor.
An invitation that looked like the breakthrough you had been waiting for.
And then God asks you a question.
“Who are these men with you?”
Your heart stops.
Because God knows exactly who they are.
He knows their names. He knows where they came from. He knows who sent them. He knows what they are carrying.
And more importantly, He knows what their offer is beginning to awaken inside you.
So why would an all-knowing God ask a question He already knows the answer to?
That is where this story becomes uncomfortable.

Because the question God asked Balaam thousands of years ago may expose something about the people we entertain, the opportunities we pursue, the compromises we justify, and the secret desires we keep trying to negotiate with heaven.
And before this story ends, something astonishing happens.
A prophet will hear from God.
A king will offer him riches.
An angel will stand in the road with a drawn sword.
A donkey will recognize danger that its rider cannot see.
And a man who knows how to speak about God will demonstrate how frighteningly possible it is to become blinded by the desires of his own heart.
But there is something even deeper.
This story eventually leads us to the difference between knowing religious truth and surrendering to Jesus Christ.
And that difference can change eternity.
The story begins in Numbers 22.
Israel had come out of Egypt. God had delivered His people from slavery, carried them through the wilderness, and brought them toward the land He had promised.
Now they were camped in the plains of Moab, across the Jordan from Jericho.
Balak, the king of Moab, was terrified.
He had seen what Israel had done to the Amorites. He knew this growing nation was not an ordinary military threat.
So he developed a plan.
If he could not defeat Israel by conventional strength, perhaps he could arrange for Israel to be cursed.
He sent messengers to a man named Balaam, son of Beor.
Balaam had a reputation for pronouncing blessings and curses.
Balak's message was unmistakable.
“Come now therefore, I pray thee, curse me this people; for they are too mighty for me.” (Numbers 22:6, KJV)
The messengers arrived carrying the rewards associated with divination.
And Balaam did something that initially sounded spiritual.
He told them to spend the night while he sought an answer from the LORD.
Then came the question.
“What men are these with thee?”
In Hebrew, the wording of Numbers 22:9 is:
מִי הָאֲנָשִׁים הָאֵלֶּה עִמָּךְ
Mi ha'anashim ha'elleh immakh?
A close translation is:
“Who are these men with you?”
The Hebrew asks about the identity of the men accompanying Balaam. The words themselves do not explicitly say that God was asking Balaam to examine his motives.
But the larger narrative invites us to examine why their presence mattered.
This was not a request for information from a God who lacked knowledge.
Scripture repeatedly reveals that God knows the human heart.
Psalm 139:1 declares:
“O LORD, thou hast searched me, and known me.”
And Hebrews 4:13 reminds us that nothing is hidden from His sight.
So when God asked Balaam about the men, the question was not evidence of divine ignorance.
It introduced a confrontation between God's purposes and the mission those men had brought.
We see something similar in the Garden of Eden.
After Adam sinned, God called to him:
“Where art thou?” (Genesis 3:9, KJV)
God did not lose Adam among the trees.
Adam had lost his innocence through disobedience.
And the question opened the moment when Adam had to answer before his Creator.
When God asked Cain, “Where is Abel thy brother?” (Genesis 4:9), God was not unaware of Abel's murder.
The question confronted Cain with the truth of what he had done.
Now God asked Balaam:
“Who are these men with you?”
And the answer was about to reveal far more than the identity of a few visitors.
It would reveal whose purposes those visitors represented.
Perhaps this is where the story begins touching your own life.
Because not every dangerous invitation arrives looking dangerous.
Sometimes it arrives through someone who praises your potential.
Someone who promises a better future.
Someone who tells you that you deserve more.
Someone who makes disobedience sound like an opportunity.
And sometimes the most dangerous invitation is not the one you immediately accept.
It is the one you refuse to stop considering after God has already made His will clear.
God gave Balaam a direct command.
“Thou shalt not go with them; thou shalt not curse the people: for they are blessed.” (Numbers 22:12, KJV)
There was no ambiguity.
Do not go.
Do not curse.
The people are blessed.
God had spoken.
And at first, Balaam obeyed.
He told Balak's representatives that the LORD refused to permit him to go.
If the story ended there, we might remember Balaam as a man who resisted temptation.
But temptation often returns wearing more expensive clothing.
Balak sent another delegation.
This time the officials were more numerous and more distinguished.
The promise became greater.
The king offered substantial honor and reward.
And Balaam responded with words that sounded remarkably faithful.
“If Balak would give me his house full of silver and gold, I cannot go beyond the word of the LORD my God, to do less or more.” (Numbers 22:18, KJV)
What a statement.
What apparent devotion.
What impressive religious language.
But then Balaam said something that should make every reader pay attention.
He invited them to stay the night so he could discover what more the LORD might say.
Wait.
Had God not already spoken?
Had He not already said that Israel was blessed?
Had He not already forbidden Balaam to curse them?
Why was another night necessary?
The text does not explicitly reveal every thought passing through Balaam's mind at that moment. We must not pretend to know what Scripture does not tell us.
But later biblical writers reveal the moral danger surrounding his actions.
Second Peter 2:15 describes Balaam as one who “loved the wages of unrighteousness.”
Jude 11 speaks of people who run greedily after Balaam's error for reward.
And Revelation 2:14 identifies Balaam with teaching that led Israel into stumbling through idolatry and sexual immorality.
The New Testament does not present Balaam as an innocent man who merely misunderstood instructions.
It exposes a heart drawn toward unrighteous gain.
And suddenly his request for another night becomes deeply unsettling.
Because there is a difference between sincerely seeking God's guidance and repeatedly revisiting a command because obedience has become expensive.
Some of us know that difference too well.
We know what Scripture says about forgiveness.
But we keep rehearsing the offense because bitterness feels justified.
We know what Scripture says about sexual purity.
But we keep calling temptation love because loneliness has become unbearable.
We know what Scripture says about honesty.
But we keep adjusting the truth because telling the whole story might cost us something.
We know we should surrender a particular ambition, relationship, habit, or hidden compromise.
But we keep asking God to show us another way.
Not because His Word is unclear.
But because our desires are loud.
And this is one of the most frightening possibilities in the Christian life:
A person can use the language of seeking God's will while secretly hoping God will approve what that person already wants.
Have you ever done that?
Have you ever prayed for guidance when, deep inside, you were actually praying for permission?
Have you ever asked God to open a door that His Word had already warned you not to enter?
Have you ever mistaken your unwillingness to surrender for a need for further confirmation?
That question is not meant to condemn someone who is genuinely confused or waiting patiently for wisdom.
God welcomes sincere prayer.
James 1:5 encourages believers to ask Him for wisdom.
But there is a difference between asking for wisdom and bargaining with obedience.
And Balaam's story warns us not to confuse the two.
Then the narrative becomes even more difficult.
In Numbers 22:20, God tells Balaam that if the men have come to call him, he may rise and go with them, but he must do only what God tells him.
The next morning, Balaam saddles his donkey and departs.
Then Numbers 22:22 says:
“And God's anger was kindled because he went.”
At first glance, this seems contradictory.
God permitted Balaam to go.
Then God became angry when he went.
How can both statements be true?
We need to handle this carefully.
The text does not provide a complete explanation of the relationship between God's conditional permission and His anger.
Some interpreters emphasize the condition in God's instruction: “If the men come to call thee.”
Others emphasize Balaam's disposition and the wider biblical testimony concerning his love of reward.
The narrative itself makes clear that permission to travel did not mean divine approval of every motive or intention Balaam carried.
And the New Testament's judgment of Balaam's greed helps us understand why his journey cannot simply be celebrated as faithful obedience.
We should not turn this passage into an absolute rule that every difficult circumstance proves God is opposing us.
Nor should we claim that God always gives people what they demand merely to punish them.
But Balaam's experience does teach a sobering lesson.
Getting the opportunity you wanted does not automatically mean your heart is right before God.
An open door is not the same thing as a holy motive.
A profitable decision is not necessarily a righteous decision.
And success is not proof that God approves of everything we did to obtain it.
That truth should humble us.
Especially in a world where people sometimes measure God's favor by money, influence, attention, and visible achievement.
Because Balaam was moving toward the reward.
And he was about to discover that the greatest danger on the road was not the distance to Moab.
It was the judgment he could not see.
The angel of the LORD stood in the road with a drawn sword.
Balaam did not see him.
But his donkey did.
The animal turned aside into a field.
Balaam struck her.
Later, the angel stood in a narrow path between vineyard walls.
The donkey pressed against the wall, crushing Balaam's foot.
Balaam struck her again.
Finally, the angel stood in a place so narrow that the donkey could not turn right or left.
So she lay down beneath him.
And Balaam, furious, struck her with his staff.
Think about that scene.
The man who claimed access to divine revelation could not perceive the heavenly danger standing directly in front of him.
But the donkey could.
The animal was trying to preserve his life.
And he punished her for it.
Then something extraordinary happened.
“The LORD opened the mouth of the ass.” (Numbers 22:28, KJV)
The donkey spoke.
She asked Balaam why he had struck her three times.
Balaam answered in anger.
And then the LORD opened Balaam's eyes.
He saw the angel standing in the road.
Sword drawn.
Judgment near.
And suddenly the journey looked very different.
The angel explained that the donkey had turned aside three times and that, had she not done so, Balaam would have been killed while the donkey was spared.
The creature Balaam had beaten had been instrumental in saving his life.
What a reversal.
What humiliation.
What mercy.
And what a warning.
Sometimes we become so consumed with reaching a destination that we resent anything interrupting our progress.
We become angry at delays.
Angry at closed doors.
Angry when someone questions our decisions.
Angry when our plans fall apart.
But not every interruption is an enemy.
Some interruptions are occasions for correction.
Some disappointments expose misplaced trust.
Some delays give us an opportunity to reconsider where our desires are leading us.
That does not mean every obstacle is a supernatural warning. Scripture does not authorize us to interpret every inconvenience as a message from God.
But it does call us to humility.
To test our desires against His Word.
To listen when correction is warranted.
To refuse the arrogance that assumes every obstacle must be removed simply because we want to move forward.
And perhaps someone reading this has been fighting against the very correction they need.
You have been angry because something did not work out.
You have been frustrated because a plan collapsed.
You have been blaming everyone around you.
But what if the most important question is not why your plans were interrupted?
What if it is whether your plans were drawing your heart away from obedience?
Balaam finally confessed:
“I have sinned; for I knew not that thou stoodest in the way against me.” (Numbers 22:34, KJV)
And yet his story did not end with that confession.
That is another important detail.
Balaam continued his journey under God's strict instruction.
When he reached Balak, the king repeatedly attempted to secure a curse against Israel.
But God would not permit Balaam to pronounce the curse Balak desired.
Instead, Balaam spoke blessings.
Again and again, Balak became frustrated.
Again and again, God's purpose prevailed.
And within Balaam's oracles came a remarkable prophecy.
“There shall come a Star out of Jacob, and a Sceptre shall rise out of Israel.” (Numbers 24:17, KJV)
In its immediate setting, this oracle announces a coming ruler from Israel who will triumph over enemies.
Within the larger biblical story, Christians have long understood its royal imagery as pointing ultimately toward the Messiah, Jesus Christ.
The New Testament does not directly quote Numbers 24:17 as a fulfilled prophecy of Jesus, so we should distinguish the passage's original setting from its later Christian messianic interpretation.
But the connection is powerful.
Even through this morally compromised figure, God declared that a ruler would arise from Jacob.
Balaam could not overturn God's blessing.
Balak could not purchase a curse that would defeat God's purpose.
And the story of redemption would continue toward the coming of Christ.
Yet here is the tragedy.
Speaking true words about God did not mean Balaam's heart was faithful to God.
Later, Numbers 31:16 associates Balaam's counsel with the events that caused Israel to stumble at Peor.
Revelation 2:14 confirms the connection between Balaam's teaching and the temptation of Israel toward idolatry and sexual immorality.
Balaam's story becomes a warning about the terrible possibility of religious knowledge without obedient love.
You can know spiritual vocabulary and still love what God condemns.
You can speak about holiness and still conceal compromise.
You can recognize divine truth and still refuse to surrender your desires.
You can appear impressive before people while remaining dangerously divided within.
And that brings us to the question we have been avoiding.
Who are these men with you?
Not because everyone around you is dangerous.
Not because Christians should become suspicious of every friendship or withdraw from unbelievers.
Jesus Himself ate with tax collectors and sinners.
He came to seek and save the lost.
The issue is not whether you associate with imperfect people.
We are all imperfect.
The issue is whether you are allowing influences, ambitions, and relationships to lead you away from fidelity to Christ.
Who has been shaping your convictions?
Whose approval are you afraid to lose?
What reward has become so attractive that you are beginning to compromise?
What secret arrangement have you made with temptation?
What have you been calling harmless even though it is slowly weakening your obedience?
And perhaps the most painful question of all:
What are you afraid Jesus will ask you to surrender?
For some, it is money.
For others, a relationship.
For others, pride.
For others, the bitterness they have carried for years.
For others, a private addiction that nobody at church knows about.
For others, the image of being spiritually strong when they are secretly exhausted and ashamed.
And maybe you are reading this while carrying something you have never told another person.
You still worship.
You still smile.
You still post Bible verses.
You still tell people God is good.
But inside, you know there is a battle.
You know there is something you have been defending.
Something you have been hiding.
Something you keep promising to abandon.
Then returning to it when nobody is watching.
And you wonder whether God is tired of you.
Whether you have gone too far.
Whether there is any hope left.
Listen carefully.
Balaam's story is a warning.
But the Gospel is the announcement of a Savior.
And the difference matters.
The Bible does not tell us that Balaam's final outcome was a beautiful story of personal repentance and restoration.
Numbers 31:8 records his death by the sword.
We must not rewrite his ending to make the story more comforting.
But we must also not confuse Balaam's judgment with the invitation God extends to sinners through Jesus Christ.
Because the good news is not that compromise has no consequences.
The good news is that Christ came to rescue sinners from the guilt and power of sin.
And this is where the story turns from the frightening road of Balaam toward the astonishing grace of Jesus.
Balaam was attracted to the rewards of unrighteousness.
Jesus rejected the temptation to gain the kingdoms of the world through worshiping Satan (Matthew 4:8–10).
Balaam needed an angel with a drawn sword to stop his destructive path.
Jesus willingly walked toward the cross, knowing the suffering that awaited Him.
Balaam's divided heart exposed the danger of loving gain more than obedience.
Jesus prayed in Gethsemane:
“Nevertheless not my will, but thine, be done.” (Luke 22:42, KJV)
Do you see the contrast?
Where human hearts are divided, Christ's obedience was perfect.
Where we have negotiated with temptation, Christ remained faithful.
Where we have loved approval, pleasure, control, and reward more than righteousness, Jesus loved the Father and obeyed Him completely.
And He did not merely come to show us what obedience looks like.
He came to save those who have failed to obey.
Romans 5:8 declares:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”
While we were still sinners.
Not after we repaired everything.
Not after we became impressive.
Not after we proved that we deserved another chance.
Christ died for sinners.
That includes the person who has spent years pretending.
The person who has repeatedly compromised.
The person who knows the Bible but has neglected the God of the Bible.
The person who has traded peace for approval.
The person who feels the unbearable weight of secret guilt.
At Calvary, Jesus carried the judgment sinners deserve.
And through His resurrection, He demonstrated His victory over sin and death.
Second Corinthians 5:21 says:
“For he hath made him to be sin for us, who knew no sin; that we might be made the righteousness of God in him.”
Jesus did not become morally sinful.
He was the sinless Savior who bore sin's judgment on behalf of His people.
And through Him, sinners can be reconciled to God.
This is not permission to continue in rebellion.
It is the grace that calls us out of rebellion.
It is not a message that holiness no longer matters.
It is the message that forgiveness and new life are possible through the One who is holy.
First John 1:9 gives this promise:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
Not merely to tolerate us.
To forgive.
To cleanse.
To restore us to fellowship with Him.
And if you belong to Christ, repentance is not the enemy of your peace.
It is part of returning to the One who loves you.
Maybe you have spent years fearing that if God exposed what was really in your heart, everything would be over.
But the cross tells us that God already knows the full seriousness of human sin.
And His grace is not based on pretending that sin is small.
His grace is revealed in the immeasurable price Christ paid to redeem sinners.
So stop hiding behind religious language.
Stop trying to make your compromise sound respectable.
Stop asking God to bless what He calls you to surrender.
Bring your heart into the light.
Not because your confession earns salvation.
But because Jesus Christ is the Savior who receives repentant sinners.
And if you are wondering whether He would receive someone as conflicted and ashamed as you, remember His words in John 6:37:
“Him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out.”
What an invitation.
What mercy.
What hope.
You do not have to remain the person you have been.
You do not have to let your worst decisions become your permanent identity.
You do not have to keep serving the desires that are destroying you.
You can turn to Jesus Christ.
Confess your sins.
Trust His finished work.
Receive His forgiveness.
And begin walking in obedience through the power of His Spirit.
There may still be consequences to face.
Relationships may need repair.
Wrongdoing may require restitution.
Some habits may require accountability, pastoral care, and practical help to overcome.
Grace does not erase every earthly consequence.
But grace changes the future of the person who comes to Christ.
That is why the Gospel Warrior message is not merely a memorable phrase.
Not because Jesus pretends the scandal never happened.
Not because He calls evil good.
Not because He promises that every broken situation will be instantly repaired.
But because He can redeem people whose lives have been devastated by sin, shame, rebellion, and failure.
He can transform the heart.
He can forgive the guilty.
He can teach the proud to become humble.
He can lead the wandering home.
And He can make someone who once lived for selfish gain into someone who now lives for the glory of God.
That is the kind of transformation worth talking about.
And perhaps this message has reached you at a moment when you needed it most.
Not to entertain you for a few minutes.
Not to make you feel guilty and then leave you without hope.
But to invite you to examine your heart before the Lord who knows you completely and offers salvation through His Son.
What is the one area of your life where you have been asking God for permission when you already know He is calling you to obedience?
You do not have to expose private details publicly.
But do not ignore the question.
Take it before God.
Someone else may need to know that repentance is possible, forgiveness is real, and no sinner is beyond the saving power of Jesus Christ.
And if someone comes forward asking for prayer, let us be a community that responds with compassion rather than condemnation.
Because the church should never make repentance more frightening than remaining in darkness.
There is another way you can help this message reach people who may never walk into a church or open a Bible on their own.
Not simply to increase its reach.
Someone may be hiding behind a smile.
Someone may be quietly losing hope.
Someone may have been told that their past makes them impossible to redeem.
And perhaps a Scripture-centered message, shared at the right moment, will encourage that person to seek Christ.
Do it with wisdom and kindness.
Never use a public tag to expose someone's private struggle.
Invite your family, your friends, believers who have grown weary, Christians who have become spiritually complacent, and even those who are still exploring the faith.
There is room here for honest questions.
There is room for people who are learning.
And above all, we want every message to lead people back to the authority of Scripture and the saving grace of Jesus Christ.
It is an opportunity to partner in the continuing work of writing, producing, sharing, and expanding Christ-centered discipleship resources.
But an important biblical distinction must remain clear.
Scripture teaches that Christian giving should be willing, thoughtful, and cheerful, not compelled by guilt.
Second Corinthians 9:7 says:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.”
Your prayers matter.
Your growth in Christ matters.
And sharing sound biblical teaching with others is also a meaningful way to serve.
These items are simply resources and reminders. They do not make anyone more spiritual, and they are never substitutes for Scripture, prayer, fellowship, or obedience to Christ.
The greater purpose is discipleship.
We want to see people learning the Word, understanding the Gospel, growing in spiritual maturity, and becoming more deeply rooted in Jesus.
These free resources reflect something we want to preserve at the heart of the ministry:
Your sharing can help the message travel further.
Your prayers can help sustain the people behind the ministry.
And together, we can keep pointing people beyond personalities, platforms, and products to the One who alone has the power to save.
Jesus Christ.
You do not glorify God by purchasing His approval. You glorify Him by trusting Christ, obeying His Word, loving others, and giving freely according to your ability and conviction.
Our mission is not to build a following that depends on us.
It is to encourage disciples who depend on Him.
And that brings us back to the night when God asked Balaam a question.
“Who are these men with you?”
At the beginning, it sounded like a simple inquiry.
By the end, it has become a mirror.
Not because God is asking every believer to fear the people around them.
But because every believer must examine what influences the heart and where those influences are leading.
Balaam heard God's voice.
He knew the language of obedience.
He spoke words of blessing.
Yet Scripture remembers him as a warning about the love of unrighteous reward.
Do not miss that.
The greatest danger in this story was not merely that Balaam encountered a tempting offer.
It was that the attraction of reward could coexist with the appearance of devotion.
And perhaps the greatest mercy you can receive today is not another opportunity.
Not another promotion.
Not another open door.
But a heart willing to say:
“Lord Jesus, I do not want anything that draws me away from You. Even if I desire it. Even if it promises me everything. Even if surrendering it hurts. Teach me to love You more.”
Because at the end of your life, the question will not be how many opportunities you pursued.
It will not be how much applause you received.
It will not be how convincingly you spoke about God.
What matters is whether you belong to Jesus Christ.
Whether you have trusted Him for salvation.
Whether your faith is bearing the fruit of repentance.
Whether the Savior you confess with your lips is the Lord you are learning to follow with your life.
And if you have wandered, do not turn this warning into an excuse for despair.
Turn toward Christ.
Today.
Not when you feel worthy.
Not when you have found the perfect words.
Not when you have repaired every mistake.
Come to Him in repentance and faith.
For the One who exposes sin is also the One who gave His Son so that sinners might be forgiven and made new.

And when you look back at the roads you should never have taken, the compromises you wish you could undo, and the moments when your heart wanted everything except obedience, may your testimony no longer be merely about how far you wandered.
May it be about the mercy of the Savior who called you home.
The most terrifying thing is not that God sees the road you are taking. It is reaching the end of that road without ever surrendering to the Savior who called you back.
